T2:
The gate closes behind him with a soft click of iron on stone.

The garden is smaller than the word 'party' had suggested — a walled square maybe forty paces on a side, the old stone wall on three sides and the gate on the fourth, espaliered pear trees trained flat against the north face, a rose arbor at the center with a bench beneath it, and a long table under a canvas awning at the west end where a pair of beast-kin servants in plain linen are laying out cold meats, bread, fruit, and a sweating pitcher of something pale. The grass is cut short and even. The air smells of crushed rose and cut grass and, faintly, of the river that runs somewhere below the property.

Anwen Drevast is standing by the arbor in a pale green dress that falls from her shoulders to her knees in one unbroken line of silk, and the dress does nothing at all to hide what she was born with. The horns curve up out of her hair, cream-gold, and her ears are the same color, and the tail hangs still behind her. She is six feet and some inches of her, and she is watching him come up the path with an expression that is not quite a smile.

'Duke Westcross. You actually came.' She says it flat, like a fact she is filing. 'I owe Callan a gold piece. He bet you would send a polite note.'

She turns without waiting for an answer and walks toward the table, and the three people standing there turn to look at him.

'Lirien Verancourt,' Anwen says, and the half-elven woman — tall, narrow, silver-blonde hair to her shoulder blades, freckles scattered across her nose and the tops of her shoulders — gives him a grin that is all teeth and no calculation at all. 'The Verancourt cousin. She is the one who will actually talk to you.'

'He's taller than they said,' Lirien says, to Anwen, not to him. 'And he's got the shoulders. I told you he'd have the shoulders.'

'Lord Aldreth Blackmoor,' Anwen says, and the man beside Lirien straightens up off the wall he had been leaning on. He is enormous — six-four and heavy with it, light grey fur thick over his shoulders and chest, his tunic open to the waist, dark hair loose and a pair of notched wolf ears swiveled toward Ryan's voice. His tail moves steadily behind him, not fast, not slow. He looks Ryan over once, from boots to hair, and does not bother to hide that he is doing it.

'Duke,' Aldreth says. His voice is a low rumble with gravel in it. 'You hunt?'

'And Sera,' Anwen says, and the third figure — a beast-kin woman in a plain grey dress, some kind of cat-kin by the ears and the slitted eyes, her fur a warm brown, maybe thirty — inclines her head. 'House Kamenova's factor in Caerveld. She is here because Vesna Kamenova wanted someone here who would notice things.'

'My lady is generous with her descriptions,' Sera says. Her voice is quiet and dry. 'I am here because I was told to be.'

Anwen picks up a glass from the table and holds it out to Ryan without looking at him, her eyes on the other three. 'There. Now you know everyone who has spent all week deciding what they think of you. The food is cold, the wine is not, and the bench under the arbor is the only seat in the shade. Sit or stand, Duke. It's your afternoon.'
T18:
Anwen does not answer right away. She sets her wine down and looks at the knife at my hip the way a woman looks at a document she has been handed and intends to read carefully.

'A ruin,' she says. 'Which one?'

'I don't know its name. It was in the north, past the marches, before I came south. I was younger than I am now and I was not there for the knife. I was there for something else and the knife was what was left of the man who had been there before me.'

That is true and it is also all I am going to say about it, and Anwen hears the shape of that and does not push. She picks her wine back up.

'And you had the fittings made,' she says. 'By whom?'

'A smith in a town I passed through. He did the brass and the guard and the pommel and he asked me three times whether I was sure I wanted the skull-crusher on the end of it. I told him three times that I was.'

'Why the skull-crusher?'

'Because sometimes the edge is not the right tool.'

Anwen's mouth moves at one corner. She drinks. She does not say anything else, but she has stopped watching the knife and started watching me, which is a different thing and I notice it.

Aldreth has not stopped watching either. He has his fork back in his hand but he is not eating with it, and his ears are forward and still.

'North past the marches,' he says. 'That's Warden country and Outmark country both, depending on which ridge you're standing on. You were in the Outmark?'

'Near it.'

'Near it.' He turns that over. 'You're a nobleman now. You were in the Outmark before you were a nobleman. That's a strange order of events.'

'It is.'

He looks at me for a beat longer than is polite, and then he does something I did not expect: he laughs. It is a short, low sound, more breath than laugh, and it is the first time he has made it.

'All right,' he says. 'You don't want to talk about the Outmark. I've been to the Outmark. I don't want to talk about the Outmark either.' He puts the fork down and picks up his wine instead. 'The knife's good. The man who made the fittings knew what he was doing. Most of the smiths in this city would have put a filigree on it and called it a family heirloom.'

Lirien has been quiet for the whole exchange, which is the longest she has been quiet since I sat down. Now she leans in over her plate with her chin on her knuckles and her eyes bright.

'North past the marches,' she says. 'Before you came south. Anwen, do you know what that means?'

'Tell me.'

'It means he wasn't in Caerveld when the Hall of Lost Houses lit up. It means he came in from somewhere else entirely and the ring found him on the road.' She looks at me. 'That's the part everyone's been trying to work out for four months, you know. Where you were. Where you came from. You've just told us a piece of it and I don't think you meant to.'

'I meant to tell you where the knife came from.'

'I know,' Lirien says, cheerfully. 'That's what makes it useful.'

Sera has finished her plate. She sets her fork down and folds her hands and looks at me across the table with the flat gold eyes, and when she speaks it is the first time she has spoken since she answered my question about her service.

'Duke Westcross,' she says. 'You said the blade was all that was left of the man who had been there before you. Did you know him?'
U27: I wake the driver, "come let's head back to the town house I'm done with this foolishness."
T28:
The driver is asleep sitting up with his hat over his face, and he does not wake when I come up the gravel, so I take the hat off him with two fingers and put it in his lap and say it once.

'Take me back to the townhouse.'

He comes awake the way drivers do — no startle, just the eyes opening and the hands already finding the reins — and looks past me at the gate, where the servant is folding the awning and the beast-kin pair are carrying the last of the plates in, and then at me, and then at the empty drive where Aldreth's grey went out ten minutes ago.

'Yes, my lord,' he says. Nothing else. He is a compact man with grey in his sideburns and a piece of straw in the corner of his mouth that he has been chewing on since Caerveld, and he has driven nobles to and from this property often enough that he does not ask which part of the party I am done with.

I get in. He clucks the horses and the carriage comes around on the gravel and out through the far arch, and the lime trees go past the windows in a slow double row and then the wall is behind us and we are on the road.

The road back runs along the river for the first mile and then turns inland through the market gardens, where the ground is dark and wet from the morning watering and there are people bent over rows with hoes and hand-carts and a woman walking a string of goats along the verge with a switch. The sun is up over the far bank now and the light comes flat across the water and into the carriage, and the leather of the seat is warm where it has been sitting in it. Nobody on the road looks at the carriage twice. A cart full of cabbages goes by the other way and the driver lifts two fingers off the reins and the carter lifts two fingers back, and that is the whole of the traffic for a mile.

The straw in the driver's mouth moves from one side to the other. He does not talk. That is a thing I have noticed about Caerveld drivers — they will talk your ear off in the city and say nothing on the road, like the horses are the only company worth having out here.

We come in through the south gate a little after the third bell and the city closes around the carriage — the smell of the tanneries first, then the bakers, then the cold stone smell of the noble quarter where the streets are wide and swept and the houses stand back behind their own walls with their own trees. The Westcross townhouse gate is open, the way it is kept open in daylight, and the carriage rolls in over the cobbles and stops under the portico and the driver sets the brake and gets down and stands at the step with his hand out for the fare, and behind him the front doors are already opening, because whoever is on the door heard the wheels.

It is a beast-kin woman — one of the household staff, tall, grey-muzzled, a wolf-kin in a plain linen apron over nothing else, which is how the whole staff dresses and has dressed since I took the house — and she holds the door and looks at me with her ears up and does not say anything, because the staff here have learned that I will tell them what I want when I want it.

The house smells like bread and beeswax and the cool of stone. The driver takes his fare and touches his hat and goes back to the box. The gate stays open behind him. Somewhere in the back of the house a door closes and a broom goes across a floor, and that is all the noise there is.
U31: I take up my bow and quiver might as well do something worthwhile while I'm in this city since this party was such a waste of time and head down to the back of the property to loose some arrows
T32:
I go down the back stairs with the bow in one hand and the quiver on my shoulder, and the house lets me out the way it lets me in — no one stops me, no one asks where I'm going.

The back of the property is a walled yard that runs the length of the stable and then opens into a strip of ground that was a kitchen garden a hundred and thirty years ago and is now just grass, cut short, with the old beds still visible as shallow rectangles in the turf. There is a stone wall at the far end, twelve feet high, running the whole width of the property, and beyond it the roofs of the next street and the top of a chestnut tree. The wall is old and the mortar is going in two places, and the staff have been using it for years — there are three arrows stuck in the mortar joints at chest height, and a fourth lying in the grass below, and the wood of them is grey and split from weather.

The wolf-kin housekeeper is in the yard. She has a basket of wet linen and she is hanging it on a line strung between the stable wall and a post, and she has one peg in her mouth. She looks at the bow and then at me and takes the peg out.

'Wall's soft at the far end, my lord,' she says. 'Left of the gate. The rest of it eats arrowheads.'

'Thank you.'

She goes back to the linen and does not watch me. That is the whole exchange.

I string the bow. It takes a moment — the recurve is stiff and the string is waxed and I have done it ten thousand times, so it goes fast, one leg through, the lower limb bent under the knee, the upper limb pulled down with the palm and the string slipped into the nock. The bow comes up taut and true and the string sits a finger's width off the limb, which is where I set it.

I nock an arrow and turn to face the wall.

Twenty-eight paces to the far end. I step it off and mark the ground with my heel and come back and stand. The wall is old stone and the light is coming across it from the left, so the joints are in shadow on one side and lit on the other, and the soft place the housekeeper named is where the mortar has gone sandy and grey and the stones sit a little proud of it. I put the first arrow into that joint.

The bow comes back to full draw and holds, and the string touches the corner of my mouth and the tip of my nose, and my hand is under my chin, and the arrow goes where I look. It is a heavy bow — sixty pounds at twenty-eight inches, built to my draw — and it takes real work to hold it, and the work is the point. The first arrow hits the joint and the shaft stands out of the wall and quivers. The second goes in beside it. The third splits the second one's nock and stands in the same hole, and I hear the housekeeper's basket go down on the flagstones behind me, and she does not say anything, but she has stopped hanging linen.

I shoot for an hour.

I do not shoot fast. I shoot the way I was taught, which is one arrow at a time, and between arrows I stand still and let the bow come down and breathe, and then I nock and draw and loose. The wall gets a line of arrows across it at chest height, and then a second line below the first, and then I start on the far corner where the light is bad and the joint is tight, and I put four into it before I miss one and the arrowhead skips off the stone and goes into the grass.

The sun comes up over the stable roof and the yard gets warm. The housekeeper finishes the linen and goes back inside and comes out once with a cup of water and sets it on the mounting block without a word and goes back in. I drink it between ends and set the cup back on the block.

By the time I stop, my shoulders are warm and my fingers are sore in the way they get sore from a bowstring and not from anything else, and there are forty-odd arrows in the wall in two ragged lines and a scatter of them in the grass below. I walk down and pull them. The ones in the soft joint come out with two fingers and a twist. The ones in the hard stone take a hand and a foot braced against the wall, and three of them come out with the heads bent and will need to be re-tipped.

I gather them all up and wipe them on my sleeve and put them back in the quiver, and I unstring the bow and coil the string and put it in my belt pouch, and I stand in the yard a minute with the bow in my hand and look at the wall.

It is a good wall. It has been taking arrows for a long time.
